3: The same logic applies to administrators, and this is where most breaches go.
A standing administrator is always on, at any hour, so any stolen credential that reaches the role gets all of it.
Stronger sign-in helps, but it doesn't narrow what the role can do, where, or when.
The role is switched on only when needed, for a set time, approved by someone else, after a fresh strong sign-in, and every elevation is logged.
NSA and sis-uh rank poor separation of admin privilege among the most common misconfigurations they find, and nist requires least privilege.
There's one standing exception: two break-glass accounts stay permanently active, so the tenant can be recovered if everything else fails.
They're safe only when governed: phishing-resistant, monitored, and tested every ninety days.

4: So what does Conditional Access actually evaluate?
First, signals: who the user is and what roles they hold, their device, the application, the location, and sign-in risk.
Conditions decide which policies apply to this particular request.
Then controls: block, or allow with requirements, like M F A, a compliant device or an app protection policy.
And session controls, such as how often to sign in again.
Three operating rules run through the library.
Every policy runs in report-only mode first, so you see its impact before it enforces anything.
Policies target personas, like admins, staff, guests and workload identities, not individuals.
And deleted policies can be recovered for thirty days.
One recent change is worth knowing: the approved client app grant went read-only on June 30, 2026, so mobile access now relies on app protection policies.
5: Underneath sit two structures: privilege and applications.
For privilege, use the least-privileged role for each task, and keep fewer than five Global Administrators, as Microsoft recommends.
Use role-assignable groups, and tier everything along Microsoft's enterprise access model, which builds on the old Active Directory tiers rather than replacing them.
For applications, the surprise is that app owners hold real admin rights over their app, including adding a credential, so keep them few.
Admin consent goes through a governed workflow, and apps authenticate with certificates or federated credentials instead of secrets.
And here's what people get wrong: consent grants never expire, and revoking one leaves tokens already issued still valid.
So application access needs the same review discipline as people.
6: Who decides access, and who carries it out?
Deciding: business and application owners decide who should have access and why, the see-so owns the policy baseline and its exceptions, and an identity governance office owns approvals and reviews.
Executing: identity engineering builds the policies and settings, the help desk handles assignments under a scoped role, and security operations handles alerts and response.
Assuring: the I S S O owns the evidence, the authorizing official owns accepted risk, and reviewers recertify access.
The rule that holds it together: the people who execute access changes never approve them.
That's why the help desk gets a custom role that manages assignments only.
The old guide gave it a role that could grant consent and act as any app, so the rule existed only on paper.
7: The policy library rolls out in five waves.
It starts with the foundation, blocking legacy authentication.
Then administrators, with phishing-resistant sign-in from privileged access workstations.
Then everyone, with an M F A baseline and device and app controls.
Then risk, blocking high-risk users and sign-ins.
And finally the remaining segments, like guests and workload identities.
Every policy passes the same gates: two to four weeks in report-only, a pilot ring, wider rings, and then enforcement with monitoring.
A wave only starts after the previous one has run a week without incident.
And rollback means switching a policy off or back to report-only, never deleting it.
The library is built to sis-uh's baseline.
It keeps the policies from Identity and Directory and adds new ones for the B O D twenty-five oh-one requirements; the slide shows the numbering.
8: For administrators, Privileged Identity Management turns privilege into a governed request.
An administrator holds an eligible assignment, not an active one.
To use it, they ask for activation with a reason and a ticket, step up their sign-in, get approval from someone else, and receive a time-boxed activation that's logged and later reviewed.
The details matter, and the old guides had several wrong.
Activation runs from one to twenty-four hours.

9: Governance means access is requested through packages with approval and an expiry date, reviews run on a tiered schedule, and guests have sponsors and get reviewed too.
As code means Conditional Access, pim settings and access packages live in version control.
Changes go through review instead of the portal, and drift is watched against a baseline.
Evidence means all of this maps to the federal access-control and monitoring controls, with every elevation and every review on record; the slide lists them.
And there are two traps in the tooling.
Reviewing an application doesn't remove members of the groups assigned to it, so the groups need their own review.
And Entra keeps sign-in and audit logs for only thirty days, so the evidence has to be exported from day one.
10: Adopt this book's Conditional Access library and wave plan as the agency's access baseline.
End standing privilege: every administrator role eligible through pim, with two governed break-glass accounts as the only standing exception.
Separate deciding from executing: name the owners, scope the help desk role, and stand up the identity governance office.
And manage access as code, with version control, review and drift monitoring, keeping the evidence from day one.
In Zero Trust, every access decision is a policy decision.
